Messages.Author: swamplor
Messages.Body:
As a result of the lengthy contestation thread, I have come to the
following conclusion.

The game of Vampire: The Eternal Struggle would be improved if cards
in players' uncontrolled regions were face up for all to see.

Advantages of this change:
1) Reduce accidental contestation. If I see that another player has
the same vampire as me in their uncontrolled region, I can choose
whether or not transfer to that vampire.
2) Increase transparency of rules adherence when an uncontrolled
vampire's capacity is relevant, such as playing Zillah's Valley,
Govern the Unaligned, or simply bringing the vampire out when its
capacity is reached.

Disadvantages
1) Making secret information public can decrease strategic depth -- I
no longer have to try to deduce which guys are in someone's
uncontrolled region (if it matters) or play around the various
possibilities.

My assertion is that the advantages outweigh the disadvantage, ergo we
should push for this change.
Who's with me?

-Steve Wampler

Messages.Author: Juggernaut1981
Messages.Body:


"I'm sorry Dave, I can't allow you to do that"

Not with you on this Steve.

Your advantages
#1: I believe this to be a cornercase event, far lower in occurrance
than "idiot play", "spiteful play" and "I'm a rush deck so I have to
rush then bitch about being neutered like a cat and then revert to
idiot/spiteful play"

#2: Most people play honestly. I haven't really had issues with
people trying to jerk you around on Zillah's, GtU@DOM, Enchant Kindred
@PRE, Founders of the Ebony Kingdom, Fourth Trad, etc. If you've got
doubts, get a judge over. If it's social play, help your playgroup do
better and play the card better. If they're a cheating jackass then
very little will probably change it even if there is transparency (the
cheating jackass will develop a new cheating method).

I am dead against "Open Crypt". Reasons follow.

#1 Mistaken Crypt
I make fairly balanced crypts in general (a few exceptions but meh).
If I draw my "smaller minions" in a non-weenie deck (say, 3cap, 4cap,
5cap, 6cap out of a crypt containing a balanced 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7,
8, 8, 8, 10, 10 spread crypt) I could be quickly labelled a "weenie
horde" and smashed off the table when I would have a hard position to
play from already.
Similar Idea if you get the "Support Cast" but no Superstar, or if you
get "All the fringe guys" and not the "Core Vamps".

#2 Crypt/Library Surprise
Many trick decks use vampires "out of character". By revealing the
'other vamps' you remove the Crypt Surprises and that bit of confusion
about what the deck does.

#3 Why Open Crypt and not Open Hand too?
All the reasons you want a hand to be closed are similar reasons for
wanting your crypt to be closed.

#4 Tactical Contesting
I can't surprise contest as a TACTICAL measure if you can see my
crypt. You'll just never bring that vampire out or I better hope like
CRAZY I can bloat fast and draw the vamp I want with "Pay 1 pool to
See 1 Vamp"...

Messages.Author: swamplor
Messages.Body:
On Aug 18, 8:16 pm, Juggernaut1981 <brasscompo...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I am dead against "Open Crypt".  Reasons follow.
>
> #1 Mistaken Crypt
> I make fairly balanced crypts in general (a few exceptions but meh).
> If I draw my "smaller minions" in a non-weenie deck (say, 3cap, 4cap,
> 5cap, 6cap out of a crypt containing a balanced 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7,
> 8, 8, 8, 10, 10 spread crypt) I could be quickly labelled a "weenie
> horde" and smashed off the table when I would have a hard position to
> play from already.
> Similar Idea if you get the "Support Cast" but no Superstar, or if you
> get "All the fringe guys" and not the "Core Vamps".

A bad crypt draw is a bad crypt draw, whether your opponents get to
see it or not.
Bad play is bad play, and there is no reason to suspect that any
particular set of information will cause bad play rather than any
other. To expand on this a little, your objection seems to be that
you might draw all little guys in a deck that isn't designed to take
advantage of such a draw and the table will gang up on you when you
are hampered anyway. That is bad play on the part of the table. Your
predator kicking you when you are down is part of the game. Anyone
else is making a mistake. I strongly suspect that giving people more
information will not, on average and in the long run, cause more
players to make more mistakes.

> #2 Crypt/Library Surprise
> Many trick decks use vampires "out of character".  By revealing the
> 'other vamps' you remove the Crypt Surprises and that bit of confusion
> about what the deck does.

True enough, additional information makes it easier to figure out what
is going on. On the whole, though, I think that's good for the game.
Sure, it is fun sometimes to see someone pull off some elaborate combo
or gimmick, but for the most part in serious play people have a pretty
good idea of the general bounds of what someone else's deck is likely
to do. And I think that's a good thing: games where someone gets
caught dramatically off guard tend to result in wild swings that do
little to reward skillful play. "If I had known he was gonna Amaranth
me, I wouldn't have blocked the bleed."

> #3 Why Open Crypt and not Open Hand too?
> All the reasons you want a hand to be closed are similar reasons for
> wanting your crypt to be closed.

As far as I can tell, the main reason to keep your hand closed is to
add an element of uncertainty to the game. If I take an action you
can react in any number of ways, depending on the cards in your hand.
For the most part, the contents of your uncontrolled region do not
affect the ways you can react. If I am contemplating bleeding you, it
is relevant if you have bounce and/or intercept and/or untap cards in
your hand. It is not relevant if you have Bear Paw in your
uncontrolled region.

> #4 Tactical Contesting
> I can't surprise contest as a TACTICAL measure if you can see my
> crypt.  You'll just never bring that vampire out or I better hope like
> CRAZY I can bloat fast and draw the vamp I want with "Pay 1 pool to
> See 1 Vamp"...

Sure, it is slightly less surprising if you do it from a face-up
uncontrolled region, but it can still be a legitimate tactical play.
Yes, a player can avoid contests by not bringing out guys others have,
but that's a feature, not a bug.

-Steve Wampler

Messages.Author: Aaron Clark
Messages.Body:
I also think that it would be a decent idea to play with an open
crypt.

Of all the solutions to "fix" unwitting vampire contestation, it is
the easiest to implement. It would require one simple rules change.
Very few existing cards would be affected, namely a couple of Group 1
& 2 Nosferatu. Those vampires would need to be errataed in order to
justify their costs.

Another plus is that it would be mechanically easier to bring an
uncontrolled vampire into the controlled region. You would not have
to remove and replace the blood counters from the card when it is
flipped over.

Admittedly, the strategy of the first few rounds of the game would
change. However, people usually know by turn three what everyone else
is playing. Would knowing on the first turn drastically change the
game environment?

Table-talk and manipulating the table verbally is a valid and I'd say
encouraged aspect of the game. My objection is that my ability to
influence the table's decisions will be hampered based on what they
know. VTES is what it is because all players are deliberately armed
with IMPERFECT knowledge. A Perfect Knowledge tactical game is Chess;
VTES is NOT Chess. Do I have an issue with my predator ousting me?
Generally nope. Do I want to give ammunition to my Predator to use
against me to manipulate the table against me (say to let my predator
have an unrestrained assault on me)? Always NO. The more "perfect"
the knowledge of players, the less table-talk and verbal manipulation
can happen.

If I get boned by my Crypt, I'd like to be able to sit there and fake
it "of course this deck runs on those minions... *discards cards
specifically for key vamps to use*"
I might have a Saulot deck, and not get Saulot at all. Problems =
many, but revealing the support cast for my Saulot deck probably makes
it look like something entirely different. (I'm sure you can think of
other cases of "key vampire + support cast"). People would play
combat differently with a Martin Frankel if they could see two more in
my crypt and an Arcane Library on the table... they would maybe try to
avoid hurting him when what I'd desperately love is Martin to explode
so I can get a new one. See closed hand.

>

"If I'd known he had Command the Beast, Foreshadowing Destruction and
Conditioning in hand I'd have blocked it or flicked it"... same issue,
different stripes.

What is wrong with rewarding the skilful play of operating a deck that
is "out of left field" and ousts using a combination people haven't
really thought about or used or perfected before? Tournaments will
always have a certain contingent of MalkS&B Cheese, Ven w/Obf, Tor
Vote, Kiyasid S&B, Ravnos Swarm Bleed, etc, etc, etc. You go into a
tournament knowing those are coming... But a deck such as Nick
Miller's "Mummies of the Inner Circle" would be easily misconstrued if
you saw the crypt (G2 ICs + FoS to make Spell of Life Mummies of the
IC vamps) and the way individuals and the table as a whole would play
would be very different. I would want to PROMOTE those decks and stop
tournaments being "Race of the Speed Bleeders".

>
> > #3 Why Open Crypt and not Open Hand too?

Of course they can affect the way I can react; just rarely how I can
react during this action. It will be how I can react to the table in
2-3 turns. You don't show your hand because a part of this game is
the threats that are contained in those cards in hand. Without those
being a mystery, is it anywhere near as easy to threaten/blackmail
someone into doing an action differently? Also, would you like me to
be playing Gisela Harden while you have an open crypt??? I'll be able
to tell VERY quickly just which vampire deserves nuking by Gisela. I
would also know just which vampires would be worth Brainwashing... or
The Name Forgotten... or...

>
> > #4 Tactical Contesting
> > I can't surprise contest as a TACTICAL measure if you can see my
> > crypt.  You'll just never bring that vampire out or I better hope like
> > CRAZY I can bloat fast and draw the vamp I want with "Pay 1 pool to
> > See 1 Vamp"...
>
> Sure, it is slightly less surprising if you do it from a face-up
> uncontrolled region, but it can still be a legitimate tactical play.
> Yes, a player can avoid contests by not bringing out guys others have,
> but that's a feature, not a bug.

There have been other proposals to fix that bug without adding that
feature.
For example "If a unique card in your uncontrolled region is already
Controlled by another Meth, you may spend 4 transfers to remove that
card from the game and move the blood to another card in your
uncontrolled region".
Fixes the bug, doesn't negate the tactical value of Contesting as a
strategic play.

I don't think the advantages you seek from an Open Crypt, using the
method you're describing, come with acceptable side-effects.

Messages.Author: Mark
Messages.Body:
I still have a hard time reading all this. Really all these proposed
changes for the scarce event of being fubar'ed out of the game when a
first-round (read first-minion) contesting occurs? Really? And now it
hase come to playing with an open crypt? Please explain to me how that
would do the game any good.

In my opinion, the whole concept of TCG's is playing with a
personalized deck of cards, kept hidden from the folks you play them
against. The thousands of option that you have by now in V:tes makes
for endless possibilities. For me, part of the fun in playing V:tes
(or TCG's in particular) is the surprise of not knowing what you're up
against. And then hope to be able to anticipate on whatever your
opponents may throw at you. Since you cannot make a deck of a thousand
cards, you are destined to be more vulnerable to certain types of
decks then others, but hey, that's part of the game. Remember M:tG? In
that game you also had to make choices. I remember a tournament in a
time when playing blue was a 'flavor-of-the-month' thing. So I
included CoP:Blue. And guess what. I never played against a blue deck
the whole tournament. Bummer. I made a choice, I had bad luck. It
wasn't a bad choice, because based on logics, it was smart including
the card. In the end, fate decided that it was obsolete in the deck.

Same goes for V:tes. You make a deck based on choices. You choose to
play certain cards (crypt or library). You do your best to prepare for
the worst. Sometimes it works out fine, sometimes it doesn't. When it
doesn't, it's not a matter of bad choices (based on the assumption
that you DO know how to make a decent deck), but more a matter of bad
luck.

The bad luck case that a majority of the latest threads seem to
address is contesting. Not even contesting in general, but the random
and rare case that someone messes up your game by contesting a big
vampire that would have been your first (correct me if I see this the
wrong way, but I assume your game is less fucked up when the
contesting concerns a low-capacity vampire - pool loss will then be
more containable).

I then understood that the issue in this case was that, how
transferring back works right now, the disadvantage (or even
punishment) is a bit too harsh, and needs some fixing.

I fail to see how playing with an open crypt fixes the problem.

Best option I have read so far is the immediate redistribution of
influenced pool to other crypt cards. That is, when a contesting
minion occurs (preventing abuse of cards like GtU and younger minions,
you get the point).

Still I'm perfectly fine with being Fubar'ed if a contest ever shows
up as described in many threads. Bad luck happens. Suck it up; better
luck next game. Never happened to me, and in all my years of play, I
had ONE of these events on a table I joined. Really, too rare for all
this fuzz.

Also, I couldn't resist commenting on this:

> Another plus is that it would be mechanically easier to bring an
> uncontrolled vampire into the controlled region.  You would not have
> to remove and replace the blood counters from the card when it is
> flipped over.

Is that really a problem for you? Try putting the influenced pool
right under the card you're influencing, indicating which minion is
intended to receive your pool. Then you just have to flip the card and
move the counters to the card, instead of first having to move the
counters off...

rules change. As it is, they are mere gravy on the addressing
contestation issue.

Messages.Author: John Whelan
Messages.Body:
On Aug 18, 7:14 pm, swamplor <steve_and_ama...@verizon.net> wrote:
> My assertion is that the advantages outweigh the disadvantage, ergo we
> should push for this change.

Let me throw in another disadvantage, before you decide.

Aside from your crypt, and your ash heap, there are 3 regions of
vampires: (1) the face down vampires; (2) the face up vampires
alongside the face-down vampires; and (3) the face-up vampires above
the face-down vampires. See diagram in rulebook.

The face-down vampires are the uncontrolled region
The face-up vampires alongside them are the torpor region
The face-up vampires above them are the ready region.

If we turn the uncontrolled vampires face up, how will we tell,
visually, which are which?

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:


Ideas:

Rotate them 180 degrees.
Use three rows: (player side) uncontrolled, torpor, ready (bank side).
Put them on one side of your pool (with the torpor region on the other side).
Put them on one side of the library (with the torpor region on the other side).

No, it's not a problem for me, I'm just throwing out an advantage of
this proposed rules change. It's not a huge advantage, but it is an
advantage. I don't usually sleeve my cards, so anything that reduces
wear and tear is welcome. Removing 10 counters from Anneke, flipping
her, then replacing the tokens is awkward, though not difficult.

Swamplor mentioned forgetting to bring out vampires from the
uncontrolled region when they're at full capacity. I hadn't thought
about it, but it happened to me recently. I had 5 blood on Blythe
Candelaria, when I thought she was Justine, Elder of Dallas. (Yes, I
was tired and lost track.) When I realized my mistake, I brought her
out and lost the 2 blood. However, she should have been influenced
out the previous turn, regardless of whether I remembered or not.

Playing with an open uncontrolled region cleans up a lot of potential
messiness.

Messages.Author: Mark
Messages.Body:


Okay, I see what you mean there. But in my experience, the biggest
issue when playing with unsleeved cards is having to use your
fingernails to try and pick 'em up from the table. Nothing more
damaging for your cards than that. So playing with sleeves would solve
that problem as well (I always advice new players to buy sleeves to
keep their cards in optimal shape).

And although I understand the fact that an open crypt would not only
potentially help against contesting, but also prevent some sloppyness
or maybe even some cheating, I still think it takes too much away from
the TGC concept of not knowing what you're up against. I'd take the
"ufo melting my rock/paper/scissor with a laser beam"-occasional and
rare contesting as an 'ah, crap...' moment, and count on better luck
for the next game I'll play.

That's the best option, I think. Except ... I've seen people turn
cards upside-down to indicate torpor: It's not a perfect practice,
since one must remember whether the card is tapped, but for whatever
reason, it is usually not a problem when I've seen it used; and it can
be helpful. I'd rather not lose that option.

Also, the time when a player is most likely to read a card is when he
is deciding whether to bring it into play. Seems unnatural for it to
be turned the wrong way -- to have to twirl them to read them and then
twirl back. I suppose someone will argue it is even more inconvenient
to be face down, but somehow, it does not seem so to me.

> Use three rows: (player side) uncontrolled, torpor, ready (bank side).

Except I frequently end up with three rows (or even 4 rows) anyway, in
order to find space for ready minions. And then you have the
locations and stuff above that. Here in NYC, we rarely get to play on
large tables, and our cards are always fighting for space.

> Put them on one side of your pool (with the torpor region on the other side).
> Put them on one side of the library (with the torpor region on the other side).

I can't see these solutions working in a space-starved environment.
The other side of my pool, or library, is where my predator's cards
go.

I'm sure it can be done, but, in the final analysis, having them be
face down just seems easier.

Maybe, but the most convenient place for my library is next to my
right hand, since I'm going to be doing alot of drawing. The most
convenient place for my pool is next to my predator, since he's the
most interested.

I need space for my crypt, and 4 cards that I draw from it. Seems
natural to put the 4 cards either to the right or the left of the
crypt, not in the center (with 2 on each side). I typically place the
library just forward of the crypt, which seems the convenient place
for it, since there is where it is out of the way of the uncontrolled
cards moving forward into the ready region (or ready cards moving
backwards into torpor). My pool the right goes of the library, next
to my predator, (if there is space) or just above it (if there isn't)
also out of the way of cards moving back and forth.

When I move one of the 4 uncontrolled cards into the ready region, a
space is left behind for a torpor region, without having to make
rearrangements.

Moving cards sideways into a torpor region, past other cards that may
be in the way, doesn't seem too convenient.
